summary: The talk presents Extended Cache Augmented Generation (ECAG) as a solution for scenarios where all documents in a collection are highly interconnected, all are relevant to answering user questions, and the dataset becomes obsolete rapidly. The speaker first evaluates Simple RAG, which uses a vector database and embedding model to retrieve similar documents via cosine similarity. While insertion is fast—enabling quick replacement of obsolete collections—Simple RAG fails when all documents are relevant because passing every document to the LLM is impractical. GraphRAG is then considered. It uses an LLM to extract entities and relationships, building a knowledge graph that connects details across the collection. This excels for stable datasets but recomputing the graph whenever data changes is computationally expensive and slow. Cache Augmented Generation (CAG) loads all documents into a model's context window and caches the KV matrix, but context windows are limited and overfilling degrades answer quality. ECAG extends CAG by using multiple parallel CAG instances, each holding a balanced, unordered subset of documents. A smarter supervisor model interrogates each bucket, progressively building understanding and asking follow-up questions to specific buckets. Documents are deliberately not organized by domains because the supervisor tends to ignore seemingly irrelevant domains when dense interconnections exist. Parallel cache loading makes the knowledge-building process significantly faster than GraphRAG and more accurate than Simple RAG. The speaker acknowledges KV cache cost concerns but notes mitigation through cache lifetime optimization, concluding that no single retrieval strategy fits all problems and each carries trade-offs in compute, cost, and speed.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem Statement
sections.summary: Luis Romero-Sevilla introduces his mission to solve knowledge representation when all context matters. He describes a scenario with a large number of interconnected documents representing events, all relevant for answering user questions, where documents become obsolete quickly and are replaced with new information.

sections.title: Simple RAG Approach and Limitations
sections.summary: Simple RAG uses a vector database and embedding model to convert documents into vectors, retrieve similar vectors for a query, and pass them to an LLM. While insertion is fast for replacing obsolete collections, it fails when all documents are relevant since passing all documents to the LLM is impractical.

sections.title: GraphRAG Approach and Limitations
sections.summary: GraphRAG uses an LLM to extract entities and relationships from all documents, building a knowledge graph that connects details across the collection. It excels for stable datasets but recomputing the graph when data is replaced frequently is computationally expensive and time-consuming.

sections.title: Cache Augmented Generation and Its Limitations
sections.summary: CAG loads all documents into a model's large context window and caches the KV matrix. However, context windows are limited and overfilling degrades answer quality, motivating the need for a distributed approach.

sections.title: Extended CAG Solution
sections.summary: ECAG uses multiple parallel CAG instances with documents distributed in balanced, unordered buckets—not by domain, since the supervisor tends to ignore seemingly irrelevant domains. A smarter supervisor model interrogates buckets, progressively builds understanding, and asks follow-up questions. Parallel cache loading makes the process faster than GraphRAG and more accurate than Simple RAG.

sections.title: Cost Considerations and Conclusion
sections.summary: KV cache is expensive but costs can be reduced by optimizing cache lifetime. No single retrieval strategy fits all problems—each has trade-offs in compute, cost, and speed. The speaker concludes by inviting further conversation and sharing contact details.

limitations: Simple RAG cannot handle scenarios where all documents are relevant—passing all documents to the LLM is impractical
GraphRAG is computationally expensive and slow to recompute when data is replaced frequently
CAG is limited by context window size, and answer quality degrades when the context window is overfilled
Organizing documents by domain causes the supervisor to ignore seemingly irrelevant domains despite dense interconnections
KV cache can be expensive, though mitigated by optimizing cache lifetime
